output.title: The hidden cost of demo theatre in a small business
output.body:
If you run a 1–10 person business, the quiet cost of demo theatre is usually not the demo itself. It is the time spent proving that a tool could work while the real workflow keeps waiting.

That matters when you keep circling the same repetitive task: customer questions, manual data work, follow-ups, or invoice handling. If the work does not repeat, AI is probably not the right place to start. No drama there; the spreadsheet can survive another week.

Bareni’s workflow diagnosis is deliberately bounded. We look for one recurring workflow, check honestly whether AI fits, and if it does, define a fixed-price pilot with clear measures. There is no mandatory roadmap gate in the middle. Pilot timings and scope are intended, not guarantees, and customers who want strategy only can use the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap.

Scope stays disciplined too: we currently decline high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work; bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests that depend on unsupported compliance or security claims. That is current scope discipline, not a claim that such work can never be automated.

A practical next step is simple: ask whether you have one repeating workflow that takes roughly 5–10 hours a week, has a measurable output, and still needs human approval for the risky part. If the answer is no, do not start with a demo.
